purpose:

content:
An update on the financial performance and
budget outturn position for 2025/26.

Councillor Sunita Gordon, Lead Member for
Resources made some introductory comments.
 
Strategic Director of Resources and Section
151 Officer introduced the report.
 
RESOLVED:
 

That the general fund revenue
outturn service overspend of £0.46m,which is offset by
£2.00m use of contingency and a £1.65m corporate costs
underspend be noted.

That it be noted that the overall
underspend of £3.19m has been used to create a £1.64m
high needs block repayment reserve and to increase the general fund
reserves by £1.55m to help support the MTFS.

That the dedicated schools grant
revenue outturn overspend for 2025/26 of £10.91m be noted and
the resulting deficit balance of £21.48m carried forward to
2026/27.

 

That the housing revenue account
revenue outturn overspend for 2025/26 of £0.04m be
noted.

 

That the 2026/27 budget delivery
assessment be noted.

 

That the capital outturn of
£107.99m be noted.

That the capital programme budget
adjustments set out in paragraphs 4.5 to 4.7 of the report be
approved.

To recommend to Full Council the
updated 2026/27 Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy for
adoption and submission to MHCLG as set out in Appendix
D.

That the Local Government and Social
Care Ombudsman decisions and actions taken as a result during Q4 be
noted.

 

That the corporate risk register and
the actions being taken to mitigate the key risks be
noted.

purpose:
This report sets out an updated Medium Term
Financial Plan for 2026/27 - 2028/29 and detailed budget proposals
for 2026/27.
content:
Councillor Sunita Gordon moved the recommendation of
the Strategy and Resources Committee.
 
Councillor Mike Dwyer moved an amendment which was
seconded by Councillor Tom
Drummond.
 
Following debate and in accordance with government
regulations recorded votes were taken on the amendment and original
recommendations the result of which was as follows.
 
RESOLVED:
 
Revenue Budget 2026/27
 

1.   
That the proposed
General Fund Net Budget Requirement of £222.088m summarised
in Updated Appendix B be agreed.


2.   
That the
Council’s pay policy statement for 2026/27 in Appendix C be
approved.


3.   
That the 2026/27
growth items in Appendix D be approved.
 
4.   
That the 2026/27
savings proposed in Appendix E be approved.
 
Council Tax and Business Rates


5.   
That the Sutton
element of the 2026/27 Council Tax at £1,868.13 for a Band D
property, an increase of £88.79 (4.99%), be agreed.


6.   
That the formal
resolution at Updated Appendix K, including the Council Tax
Requirement of £143.120m, be approved.


7.   
That the proposed GLA
precept of £510.51, an increase of £20.13 (4.1%), due
to be agreed by the London Assembly on 26th February 2026, be
noted.
 
Other
 

8.   
That the
Members’ Allowances Scheme for 2026/27 (Appendix G) be
approved.
 

9.   
That the Fees and
Charges proposed for 2026/27 (Appendix H) be approved.

10.That the Equalities Impact Assessment of the budget
proposals (section 24) be noted.
 

11.That the Climate Impact Assessment of the budget proposals
and the Climate Budget presented in Appendix M, be
noted.
 
Capital Programme
 

12.That the new Capital Strategy (Appendix I1) including the
detailed Capital Programme (Appendix I2) for 2026/27 to 2029/30
with a total spend of £375.818m (General Fund £149.300m
and Housing Revenue Account £226.518m), including the
proposed funding arrangements and policies, be approved.
 

13.That an increase to the proposed allocation of capital
receipts to 50% of 2025/26 receipts to fund Transformation Spend as
set out in the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Forecast in
Appendix I3 be approved.
 
14.That the approach taken to resource the transformation
programme including a time limited market supplement as set out in
paragraph 21.7, be noted.
 
Treasury Management
 

15.That the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 including the
Annual Investment Strategy, prudential indicators, Minimum Revenue
Provision (MRP) policy and borrowing limits (Appendix J) be
approved.
 
Reserves

16.That the forecast reserves position as set out in section
23 be noted.

purpose:
This report sets out an updated Medium Term
Financial Plan for 2026/27 - 2028/29 and detailed budget proposals
for 2026/27.
content:
Councillor
Sunita Gordon, Lead Member for Resources made some introductory
comments.
 
The
Strategic Director of Finance, Section 151 Officer, introduced the
report and gave an update on the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit
and high needs grant funding, following an announcement by the
Government, made after the report was published. 
 
RESOLVED:
 
To
recommend to Full Council the following decisions related to the
Council Tax Decision for 2026/27: Revenue Budget
2026/27 




To agree the proposed General Fund Net Budget
Requirement of £222.088m summarised in Appendix
B. 

 


To approve the Council’s pay policy statement
for 2026/27 in Appendix C. 


To agree the 2026/27 growth items in Appendix
D.


To agree the 2026/27 savings proposed in Appendix E.
Council Tax and Business Rates 


To agree the Sutton element of the 2026/27 Council
Tax at £1,868.13 for a Band D property, an increase of
£88.79 (4.99%). 


To approve the formal resolution at Appendix K,
including the Council Tax Requirement of
£143.120m. 


To note the proposed GLA precept of £510.51,
an increase of £20.13 (4.1%), due to be agreed by the London
Assembly on 26th February 2026. 

 
Other 




To approve the Members’ Allowances Scheme for
2026/27 (Appendix G). 

 


To approve the Fees and Charges proposed for 2026/27
(Appendix H). 


To note the Equalities Impact Assessment of the
budget proposals (section 24).


To note the Climate Impact Assessment of the budget
proposals and the Climate Budget presented in Appendix
M. 

 
Capital
Programme 
 


To approve the new Capital Strategy (Appendix I1)
including the detailed Capital Programme (Appendix I2) for 2026/27
to 2029/30 with a total spend of £375.818m (General Fund
£149.300m and Housing Revenue Account £226.518m),
including the proposed funding arrangements and
policies. 





To approve an increase to the proposed allocation of
capital receipts to 50% of 2025/26 receipts to fund Transformation
Spend as set out in the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Forecast
in Appendix I3 


To note the approach taken to resource the
transformation programme including a time limited market supplement
as set out in paragraph 21.7. 

 
Treasury Management 
 


To approve the Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27
including the Annual Investment Strategy, prudential indicators,
Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) policy and borrowing limits
(Appendix J). Reserves 

 


To note the forecast reserves position as set out in
section 23. 

 
The Strategy & Resources Committee
resolved: 
 


That the capital delivery plans for the Digital
Programme and Corporate Asset Investment Programme set out in
Appendices I4 and I5 to the report be approved.


That the decision taken under S151 Officer delegated
authority not to join a Business Rates Pool for 2026/27 be
noted.


That the schools funding formula factors as set out
in Appendix F be approved.

 


That the allocation of the crisis and resilience
fund (as set out in section 7.21) be approved. 

 


That the rent increase of CPI + 1%, which is in line
with the government’s cap on social rent increases in
2026/27,  be noted and that the
budget proposals set out in Appendix L1 for the Housing Revenue
Account (HRA) be approved, which were presented to the Housing,
Economy and Business Committee in January 2026.


That the updated assessment of compliance against
the CIPFA Financial Management Code as set out in Appendix A
be noted.

(except points 4 and 5 under Council believes)
 
Council consented to the alteration.
 
Councillor Jake Short moved the altered amendment
which was seconded by Councillor Sam
Cumber.
 
Councillor Wendy Clark moved the remaining aspects
of the amendment which was seconded by Councillor Catherine Gray.
 
Following debate, the amendment was put to the vote and
lost, the altered amendment was put to the vote and
carried.
 
RESOLVED:
 
Council Notes: 


The London Cancer Hub is estimated to generate
£1.2bn to the UK economy annually when fully operational
alongside 13,000 jobs in the health, science, education and
construction sectors in the borough and is a key pillar of the
London Growth Plan. 

According to recent data via City Hall’s High
Street Data Service, Sutton Town Centre has, since the COVID-19
Pandemic, seen a faster recovery of footfall and reductions in
vacant commercial units than London as a whole. 

Occupancy rates in Sutton Town Centre are
significantly higher than the London average at
92%. 

There are currently over 1,100 households housed in
Temporary Accommodation by the London Borough of Sutton, and across
London there is a significant crisis in housing and temporary
accommodation.

The Government has routinely linked house-building
to economic growth. 

Despite this, private sector housebuilding across
London has slowed significantly in recent years. This is driven by
rising construction costs, and reduced buyer affordability, which
have undermined scheme viability and stalled delivery.

In previous decades, large-scale council house
building delivered genuinely affordable homes across the capital
and the country as a whole. 

The Council has delivered 161 new council homes
across the borough in recent years, including the most recent
completion of 9 new homes at 30-32 Beddington
Lane. 

The recent launch of Sutton’s Economic Growth
Plan placed particular emphasis on providing new affordable homes
in an area-appropriate way and on the influence of providing skills
for Sutton residents to ensure the economic success of the
borough. 

Both the Council and the Greater London Authority
(GLA) have a role to play in promoting economic growth, jobs and
skills training in Sutton. 

The GLA has recently launched an Inclusive Talent
Strategy and taken on management of the Department of Work and
Pensions’ ‘Connect To
Work’ programme in London. 

Developer contributions from housing are a key way
to deliver new infrastructure that benefits all Sutton residents
including safeguarding space for new health infrastructure and
building new schools like the Harris Academy in Belmont and two new
SEND schools in the borough.   

 
Council Believes: 


The delivery of projects like the London Cancer Hub
will provide thousands of well-paying local jobs; deliver much
needed economic growth for the UK economy and put Sutton on the map
as the global home of oncology. 

In building housing in a way that is appropriate for
the different towns and districts that make up the London Borough
of Sutton. 

The delivery of more genuinely affordable council
housing across the borough is the only way to tackle the Housing
Crisis.

New homes should be built to the highest possible
environmental standards including Passivhaus standards 

New homes are a key part of increasing footfall,
delivering infrastructure and ensuring the economic success of our
town and district centres. 

Private development must also provide benefits to
local residents including through job opportunities during
construction.

It has an important role to play in shaping the
local economy through targeted acquisitions and other interventions
to bring vacant units back into use and through the development of
local skills and employment opportunities, while delivering value
for money to the tax payer.

A locally-led planning system is a vital part of
giving local control over all of the above. 

New measures being introduced by City Hall and the
Government supposedly to expedite new house-building in London are
fundamentally flawed and will not deliver the homes London
needs.

 
Council Resolves: 


To continue to deliver the goals of the recently
adopted Economic Growth Plan including lobbying and working with
the GLA member for Sutton and Croydon for significant public
transport investment from City Hall and recognition from the
Government of the national significance of the London Cancer
Hub. 

To develop a Local Supplier Directory identifying
local construction businesses and encourage private developers and
the Council itself to use that directory. 

To promote the Connect To
Work programme to local businesses and identify opportunities to
use the programme within the Council. 

To enhance our borough’s reputation as a good
place to invest and do business, supporting sustainable growth,
attracting new employers and bringing new jobs and prosperity for
our residents. 

To continue work with partners to bid for enabling
funding such as the Local Innovation Partnership Fund wherever such
pots of funding arise, to boost productivity, attract investment,
and create skilled jobs.

Continue to support the London Festival of
Architecture’s involvement in the borough recognising its
role in promoting high quality design, supporting local businesses,
and raising the borough’s profile as a place for innovation
and investment.

To further develop the Green Enterprise Partnership
to encourage local businesses to meet high environmental standards
by providing targeted support, guidance, and incentives that help
local businesses improve environmental performance, reduce carbon
emissions, and meet high environmental standards while remaining
commercially viable.

To robustly oppose the moves from Central Government
to remove local decision making over the planning system including
the emergency measures already announced and to defend the role of
local authorities in shaping sustainable development that reflects
local needs and protects our parks and green spaces.

To continue to deliver more affordable housing
across the borough to the highest environmental standards whilst
ensuring value for money for the hard
working Sutton tax payer.

To acknowledge that public confidence in
regeneration and housing delivery depends on sound financial
stewardship, and to commit that no future housing, energy or
regeneration project will proceed without realistic assumptions,
full transparency of risk, and compliance with best-practice
financial governance standards as identified by CIPFA.
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for the development of the London Cancer Hub, affordable housing, and economic growth in Sutton, despite contentious issues surrounding private sector interests and government policies.

content:
The motion was moved by Councillor Andrew Jenner and seconded by
Councillor Tom Drummond.
 
Following debate the motion was
put to the vote and carried.
 
RESOLVED:
 

“By talking about cancer, in all
its guises, we make it more normal. We can break down taboos and
stop people feeling embarrassed. The difference between an early
and late diagnosis is the difference between life and death in many
cases”  ?
Dame Deborah James, 1 October 1981- 28 June 2022 (age
40 years)
 
Council notes that:
(i) bowel cancer, which
includes both colon and rectal cancer, is the fourth most common
cancer in England and the second biggest cancer killer.
Approximately 63% of cases occur specifically in the
colon.
(ii) while 94% of cases are diagnosed in those over
50, there is a rising incidence of colon cancer among younger
people (under 50), who often present with more aggressive forms of
the disease.  Over the last few
years, the number of young adults diagnosed with bowel cancer has
been on the rise. Between the early 1990s and 2018, the number of
adults aged 25 to 49 being diagnosed with bowel cancer  increased by 22% in the
UK.

(iii) early diagnosis is critical; 91%
of patients survive five years or more if diagnosed at Stage 1,
compared to only 11% at Stage 4. Currently, only 40% of patients
are diagnosed at Stages 1 or 2, significantly trailing the national
ambition of 75%. 

(iv) 54% of bowel cancer cases are
preventable, with key risk factors including diet, obesity,
smoking, and alcohol.  Environmental factors have been associated with the
disease. These mayinclude
sedentary lifestyle, being overweight and obesity, smoking, heavy
alcohol use, low-fibre, and high-fat diets or diets high in
processed meats. 
  

Council resolves to:
(i) collaborate with
The Institute of Cancer Research on local messaging for World
Cancer Day on 4 February, which will include specific information
on bowel cancer.
(ii) actively support NHS partners, including Royal
Marsden Partners, NW and SW London NHS Cancer Alliance who are
launching a two-week London-wide campaign on bowel cancer screening
in February.
(iii) work with our Charity, Faith and
Community sector colleagues and NHS partners to deliver a community
engagement event for Bowel Cancer Awareness Month in
April.
iv) continue to work with local
partners to promote healthy lifestyles, including healthy diets, in
order to help prevent future cases of bowel cancer
v) The Director of Public Health to elevate awareness
among local GPs and strongly encourage prompt consultation upon the
discovery of potential signs, given the significant increase in
bowel cancer incidence among the under 50s
 
The Council calls for the Government and the NHS
to:

(i) Publish
the detailed National Cancer Plan for England as a matter of
urgency. While the broader 10-Year Health Plan was released in July
2025, a specific, fully-funded roadmap is essential to translate
those high-level ambitions into a clinical reality for cancer
patients.

(ii) To bring the age of testing down
to 45 in line with countries like Australia.  To implement
automatic screening for individuals with a family history of bowel
cancer.

(iii) Implement a fully funded action
plan to tackle chronic staff shortages in endoscopy and pathology
services. These vacancies represent the single biggest barrier to
delivering world-class bowel cancer care and meeting diagnostic
targets.

(iv) provide all bowel cancer patients
with detailed genetic testing, including routine screening for
Lynch syndrome and other genetic biomarkers, to ensure they receive
the most effective, targeted treatments.
topline: The Council has decided to take action on bowel cancer, including raising awareness, promoting early diagnosis, and calling for government support.

The Mayor announced that there had been a technical change
to the original motion which was agreed
by Council.
 
Councillor Tony Shields moved the motion which was seconded by Councillor Param
Nadha.
 
Councillor Jake Short moved an amendment which was seconded by Councillor Richard Clifton.
 
Following debate the amendment was put
to the vote and carried. The amended motion was put to the vote and carried.
 
RESOLVED:
 
Council notes:

·        
The growing concern
among residents about the increase in Houses in Multiple Occupation
(HMOs) across the borough and the associated impacts on parking,
refuse management, noise, and local amenity.

·        
That the number of
licensed HMOs among private rented households in the London Borough
of Sutton increased  in recent years but
licensing changes in 2018 make comparisons with prior to that date
misleading as the scope of what constitutes a HMO changed
significantly.  

·        
That if current trends
continue, the number of HMOs in the borough may almost double over the next ten
years.

·        
That HMO licensing and
planning permission operate under separate legislative regimes, but
in practice there is significant overlap
between the two. An HMO licence
is often sought for a property that also
requires planning consent. The absence of coordination between
these processes can cause confusion and inconsistency.

·        
That local authorities already hold powers under the Housing Act
2004 to refuse or revoke HMO licences
where the licence holder or property
fails to meet the required standards, or where the use of the
property breaches planning control and enforcement action has been
taken. Other councils, including Coventry City Council and Rhondda
Cynon Taf
County Borough Council, actively use these powers. This Council
therefore recognises the importance
of applying them locally and consistently to
uphold planning control and housing standards.

·        
The introduction of an
Article 4 Direction in Sutton, by the Liberal Democrat
administration, to withdraw permitted development rights for the
conversion of family homes into smaller HMOs is
welcomed. This measure restores local planning scrutiny and
ensures that such changes are properly assessed against planning
policy and neighbourhood amenity
considerations after the previous Conservative led government
de-regulated this area of planning law.

·        
That the Liberal
Democrat administration recently consulted on additional licensing
measures for HMOs building on the progress made with the Article 4
Directive to ensure that HMOs are of a decent standard.
 
Council regrets:
·        
That as a consequence of Conservative austerity, written
notifications to residents of local changes, including conversions
to HMOs and associated planning applications, are no longer
routinely issued.
 
Council further notes:

·        
That this change was
accompanied by the development of an online notification system
that has led to an increase in participation in the planning
process from Sutton residents, allowing residents to be notified of
any application they might be interested in anywhere in the
borough, not just in their immediate area.

·        
That ward councillors have a crucial role to play for
residents who are not able to access the online notification
system.
 
Council therefore resolves:

·        
That where an HMO
planning or licence application is
received, the Council will ensure that written notification is sent
to all properties within a 100-metre radius of the application
address, informing residents of the application and providing
details on how to submit comments or raise concerns, as soon as the
Conservative austerity that forced this change is
reversed.

·        
In the absence of
this, to continue to encourage ward councillors to see as an important part of their
role, the active monitoring of planning applications in their wards
including those relating to HMOs in order to inform residents and
provide details on how they can submit comments and raise
concerns.

·        
That the
Council’s HMO Licensing Policy be updated to clearly state
that applicants are expected to seek and obtain planning consent
where required, before or alongside applying for a licence.

·        
That the Council
continues to ensure that, where a property is subject to planning
enforcement action or a final enforcement notice has been served, this information is fully
considered by the Licensing Team when assessing the suitability of
any HMO licence application or renewal.
This should include cases where the breach impacts the “fit and proper person” test
or the safety and suitability of the accommodation, in line with
the Housing Act 2004 and all due process.
topline: The Council has decided to address the increase in Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) and associated impacts on the borough.

content:
The motion was moved by Councillor Barry Lewis and seconded by Councillor Isabel Araujo.
 
During the debate Councillor Drummond proposed that the question now
be put which was seconded by Councillor
Wendy Clark. The procedural motion was put to
the vote and lost.
 
Following debate the motion was put to
the vote and carried.
 
RESOLVED:
 
Council notes:
(i) in Sutton we celebrate the fact that we are a
diverse, inclusive, respectful and welcoming community where people
of all cultures and national backgrounds get along and
thrive.
(ii) Sutton has had a deserved reputation as a community
that has welcomed people fleeing persecution, in particular in
recent years those from Afghanistan, Ukraine and Hong
Kong.
(iii) Sutton has recognised and
celebrated the important contributions people from a range of
different cultural and national backgrounds have made to our
society and to our workforce, particularly in the care sector and
in local hospitals.
 
Council further notes:
(i) that there has been an
increase in extreme narratives and support for those narratives
over the last 15 years, as seen through increases in Islamophobia
and antisemitism, and more recently, the focus on migrants,
refugees and asylum seekers.
(ii) with concern the way
statements and policies associated with some political leaders have
created uncertainty and fear, particularly the suggestion that
those with indefinite leave to remain in our country and who have
lived and worked here for many years may find their status changed.
This contributes to concerns that they may be
threatened with deportation, breaking up long established
family units and losing experienced people from their
jobs.
(iii) with concern the recent
terrorist attack on the synagogue in Manchester and the appalling
arson attack on the mosque in Peacehaven and the impact that these have had on
many of our communities in Sutton.
 
Council resolves
(i) to offer reassurance to all our communities in
Sutton and to reiterate its support for a respectful and inclusive
society.
(ii) to continue to work
alongside the police and our charity, community and faith sector to
build community cohesion.
(iii) to write to the Home
Secretary to urge them to provide support and resources to local
authorities to help build community cohesion and oppose racism,
hate, hostility and anti-migrant sentiment.
topline: The Sutton Council has decided to reaffirm support for a diverse and inclusive community amidst rising extremism and political uncertainty.

offset the impact of high inflation on benefits.
 
The Committee was informed that the draft
Funding Strategy Statement (Appendix B) had been reviewed and
updated to align with new CIPFA and Scheme Advisory Board guidance.
Members then discussed the process to follow. Officers confirmed
that following the Committee's approval of the draft, the next step
was to begin the formal consultation with all scheme employers. It
was explained that the draft FSS would be sent out alongside the
initial individual employer results from the actuary, which was the
next stage of the valuation process
 
Members also discussed the key actuarial
assumptions recommended in the report, including the decision to
increase the prudence level from 70% to 85% and the adoption of a
long-term CPI inflation assumption of 2.3% p.a.
 
Members also discussed the data quality in
relation to the triennial valuation. Officers confirmed a
significant improvement in data quality since the 2022 triennial
valuation. The Fund Actuary, who was present, agreed with Officers
and advised the Committee that the data provided was considered
“healthy”, providing a sound basis for the valuation
results.
 
RESOLVED:
 

1.   
To approve the draft Funding Strategy Statement (Appendix B).

2.   
To note:
·        
the initial whole Fund results;
·        
the proposed valuation assumptions;
·        
Prudence level of (at least) 85% is adopted, which results in a
future investment return assumption (‘discount rate’)
of at least 5.3% per annum (pa);
o  
CPI inflation assumption is set using best estimate inflation
projections from the Actuary’s model, resulting in a CPI
assumption of 2.3% pa
o  
Longevity assumptions are set in line with the Fund Actuary’s
best estimate assumptions, as supported by Club VITA analysis
o  
All other demographic and financial assumptions are set in line
with Actuary’s best estimate assumptions.
o  
the potential impact of post 31 March market volatility and that
the proposed assumptions and employer funding plans remain
appropriate for the 2025 valuation.
